claim.pdf_says:
c) If any of the file description entries has a LINAGE clause, all shall have a LINAGE clause specifying
    1. the same corresponding values for any literals specified
    2. the same corresponding external data items.
claim.markdown_says:
c) If any of the file description entries has a LINAGE clause, all shall have a LINAGE clause specifying

   1\. the same corresponding values for any literals specified

   2\. the same corresponding external data items.
claim.why_it_matters: In 13.3.4.3 GR2, the numbered sub-items 1. and 2. are printed nested under subrule c); the markdown indents them at the same level as a)-e), detaching them from their parent subrule. The wording survives, so the meaning is recoverable from the run-on sentence.

verdict.reasoning: Printed page 236 (PDF p258), 13.3.4.3 GR2 c): the sub-items '1. the same corresponding values for any literals specified' and '2. the same corresponding external data items.' are indented one level deeper than c). The markdown (page-258.md lines 31-35) carries the same items, in the same order, with identical wording, directly after c)'s run-on lead-in 'specifying', and before d). The only difference is indentation depth (3 spaces, same as a)-e)), which is formatting. Nothing is missing, reordered or misattributed: the items follow c)'s unfinished sentence and precede d), so they can only belong to c). The claim itself concedes the meaning is recoverable. This is indentation, not a content discrepancy.
